fullContext:
Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Hey, everyone, and welcome back to the Information, uh, Bottleneck Podcast. And today we have Zhuang Liu. He's a assistant professor, uh, at Princeton. Hi, Zhuang. Nice to have you.

Zhuang Liu: Hi, Ravid. Mm. Hi, Alan. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And as always, we have Alan. Hey, Alan.

Allen Roush: It's good to see you again, Ravid. Nice to meet you, Zhuang. And, uh, yeah, you should go take a look at his Google Scholar. He has a lot of really cool papers.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Yeah, so we'll talk about some of these papers, uh, today. And in general, we are going to talk about what are the important components, uh, in today AIs. Okay? So you have so, Zhuang, you have so many works. Uh, I think we can start with some understanding of what do you think are the important component. So, uh, a few years ago, you had a paper about, uh, a conv, a convnet for the 2020s, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, that, you know what? Maybe you'll tell us about what is the, the paper about, and then we can start to, to start to decompose the-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... the components for current, uh, AI systems.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Yes, of course. So that was a really interesting story. So the paper, we, we were working on this paper in twen- 2021, and back then, transformers has just entered the computer vision's, world, computer vision research space, through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community have, have been, switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they are getting better and better performance. So in, so in this work, we want to say, we want to investigate, whether truly, like, convnet is, has lost its, competitiveness, and whether it's possible to, to, control all the design components there is to study whether convnets can be modernized to be, on par with vision transformers at that time.

So we wanna study whether it's a, it's a difference that seeming, seemingly, performance gap between transform- vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution or due to other small, like seemingly small design details. So, and we found the answer to be, the latter. So after a lot of studying, in, of like modernizing the design compon- components of a convnet, we eventually get the model to be on par with, vision transformers, very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that, no matter you choose convnet or vision transformers, as long as you get the des- the, everything correct, you'll, you'll get, the same frontier level performance on vision tasks.

Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And do you still believe that this is true? Do you still believe that like at the end, it doesn't really matter?

Zhuang Liu: I wouldn't s-- Yeah, I, I largely tend to agree, but I wou- I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. it's, I, I would say, as long as you get everything correct, like as long as you have, y- explore the s- the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's like kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. like I think in the past, many years, there haven't been real- really, like innovations that, have been widely adopted other than the, kind of the mature architectures that we, we already were working with, several years ago. but, but this process itself is very, very fun. in fact, recently there have been some, paper releases on this, especially from this, open, open weight model companies like Kimi, DeepSeek.

They're still playing around with architectures, like how do you, how do you change residual connections? How do you, connect different layers? these kind of stuff. And, and I respect that work a lot. In fact, part of the reason that architecture research is less active in academia right now is that, we couldn't really afford to, afford the compute to demonstrate these effects in, in, convincing scale. So that's a, a sad part, but I still try to play around with it myself using our, resources at, at, university. actually, with the help of Cloud Code, I can now, go back to coding to, to play around in the first hand myself. So this is very fun research, but in, I do think in, from a practical stand, point of view, what data we learn, what data we train the model on matters more than, the architecture choice.

As long as the interface, the input/output interface stays the same, architecture, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The, the very basic function of, of neural networks or deep learning. And how we parameterize it, no matter, as long as you get like a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or, or other like, reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward, layers at the right places, you'll be at the f- very close or at the frontier, curve of this, performance, versus efficiency, balance. And, then I was, I, I would tend to think that what, what matters more in terms of practical usage, in terms of bringing the product to more and more people to be more effective in their daily usage.

I do think other, other aspects like what data has this model been trained on, how it can handle context and memory is what, what matters more. So in terms of context and memory, yes, there are-- there do exist architectural work that, address that. So I think that is kind of the more immediate problems we, we need to address in, in making AI like up another level. Yeah.

Allen Roush: In a ConvNet for the 2020s, uh, first of all, you know, maybe just give your summary of that paper, but, but then my, my question is, um, you know, as I read it, uh, it looks like you, you gr-- and also correct me if this, uh, uh, my understanding is wrong, but my understanding is you gradually modernize ResNet towards a Swin-like design and end up-

Zhuang Liu: Right

Allen Roush: ... with a ConvNet that competes strongly with transformers. Um, which single ablation did you, like in that paper, most changed your own mind about where the supposed transformer advantage was really coming from?

Zhuang Liu: what ablation? I think it's every ablation. If you, if you look at the graph, nothing single-handedly, transformed, like brought, brought up the performance by large margin. Like some of them are more useful than others, but, it's not really that one change changed everything. maybe the, I, I guess the use of activation and norm-- redu-reduction of normalization layers is one thing that, kind of intrigued me and, has a noticeable performance change. but it was really everything together. So these seemingly small components, when we compound them together, they can, they can really cause large differences that would normally attribute to, some, some substantial change, like changing convolution to a self-attention or in, into, modernized, say, more modern mechanisms like linear attention, right?

So, so I think the, the big lesson here is, these small details when combined together matters much more than the sim- seemingly core components of the networks. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: But do you think it's-- because for me, it looks that like we have, like we are trying a lot of things. Some of these things are working, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then we get better models.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: And then like in retrospective, like we can, we can start like to understand like exactly what the component that are actually matter, right? Like we can-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... try to, oh, so now let's change ConvNet and, and make it look, looks more as a, as a transformer, for example, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Um, do you agree with that? Do you think that like this is something that we actually need, need this breakthrough, and then we can trace back and, uh, understand the, the details and try to match other methods? Or do you think like we just need to try again and again, and, uh, we don't need the very specific, uh, directions?

Zhuang Liu: I see. Got it. Yeah, I think transformer absolutely is a blessing to the, to the community and also the vision transformers, the, the adoption of transformers in computer vision. I don't debate that. That's, that's hard to debate. it's, it's absolutely a breakthrough, a very important breakthrough. perh- perhaps the, the biggest breakthrough in, in that, years. and, so our study was more focusing on like computer vision only domains. But another benefit of vision transformers is that they, they allow the unification of, of text and image representations, right? it's, it's then the use of transformer is very important for later developments like, LLaVA, like this multimodal framework where you have text enc-- vision encoders encode the vision into tokens, and then just treat tokens, get them together to be fed into a, a downstream LLMs.

It's a basic framework of a lot of multimodal models right now. So I think, the adoption of transformers in vision is v- a big stamp, big step for unification of multimodal data. This is, back to the, our study. Investigation of details, I, I would say it's more of a lesson. It's l- not, I think it changed my understanding more than, more than like... I'm, I'm more proud of this work because it changes my own understanding and some other, a lot of other people's understanding rather than like we now can go really, like you can still stay with ConvNets. I, I-- people can still do that. The ConvNets has its own benefits as well, especially when, restricted to computer vision only.

It's, it's convenient to deploy. It's, kind of easier to understand, especially it, may also have, better support for higher resolution long con-- long, long sequences because the operation is local. I, I, I think they just excel at different places. and this, this study-... transformation of details is a, a, is more kind of a lesson for me rather than like, we need to figure out each component, how, how much they contributes to, to performance, difference. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So, okay. So these are, uh, okay, so, so architecture is not so important, and you also like you have a more recent paper that you actually showed that, uh, uh, normalization layers are not so important, right? That you can basically can, um, remove normalization layer using, uh, um, uh, a tangent, uh, um, activation function, right? And, and maybe you need to do, uh, some tweak and, and to, to, to treat it a bit differently, but-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it works fine.

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: So what do you think is the, what do you think are the important components and, you know, the core components that you say like, okay, these are so important for AI, for deep learning, and, and why Only in the recent years, like we, we came up with such good models. Well, why-- if, if architecture, um, doesn't matter, why we only have good AI models in the last, like, five years or 10?

Zhuang Liu: Yeah. it's a good question. Yeah. so first, transformers was brought up into the world 10 years ago, nine years ago. so it was a long time before. And even after that, we, we still follow like a similar fundamental framework right now with, with some minor changes like activation layers, mix of expert, mixture of experts that's not always needed, and also some change on how, like local attention, sliding window attentions. But the same, frameworks is still the same as, nine years ago when the paper initially came out. So I think that's the answer to that would be, for me, it would be just the s- the data, the scale of data we train them on, the scale of compute we use to train them. like, like it's, it's, like the, the classic story from GPT-1 to GPT-3, right?

Once you try and train the model, train the basically the same model using more compute, more data, more diverse data, more, internet scale data, we all get this emerging very competitive, performance we, we see now. So I would attribute that to, to, to, to the data and, and also secondarily to the, to the compute, to the how, how, how many, epochs we train on the same data. I think, I think actually, it's mostly data because now we train most models with less or just equal around, around one epoch. Yeah.

Allen Roush: I, I, I see that this thesis permeate through your work about, uh, the field is confounding architecture with recipe, right?

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm.

Allen Roush: Specifically in your ConvNext paper, um, right? If you were setting rules for like architecture papers today, and maybe you do these exact rules for your students-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Allen Roush: ... what controls would you require, right, before someone can claim that some inductive bias-

Zhuang Liu: Okay

Allen Roush: ... some, especially like a new one matters?

Zhuang Liu: Got this. ideal, in ideal world, we would have unlimited compute, right? So, so first of all, I would require, I would require the effect, the benefit to be demonstrated on a, on a state-of-art scale, like, like, not necessarily frontier models, but like 7B, 30B. Yeah, but, I think scale is, is important for industry to really, see the benefit, to be convinced about the, the change, the benefits. But that's not always possible, so I wouldn't-- it's just, in ideal world. But secondly, if you want to study these mechanisms, architecture changes in smaller scales, like the ones we could do in, reasonable resource, with reason- reasonable resources, I would s- I would require first, hyperparameter sweep. we need to-- we, we, we cannot, demonstrate the, the new architecture just on one set of-- it works on one set of hyperparameters better, than the old model, especially when that hyperparameter is tuned just, just for that model. so ideally every-- so each model should compare against each other on their own best hyperparameter settings.

And the most important hyperparameters would be learning rate, weight decay, optimizers with the optimi- optimizers, optimizer types. And, it just bothers me a lot when people re- don't even tune the learning rate and, and then claim like-- people only tune the learning rate of their own method without tuning the learning rate of the baseline. That's kind of the, the easiest, like most, common fix for a lot of, claims that, that, turn out not to be generalizing. that's for one. And secondly, I would require the, the idea or the method to be demonstrated on more than one dataset, especially on, it should be on reasonable scale dataset. I would say ImageNet is still applicable today, but ideally they should also demonstrate the idea to work on, some, some small scale large language models, say for, for example, training on FineWeb.

But I understand that not every lab has the resource to do that. But I, I, I'm a big fan of like demonstrating ideas on a diverse range of datasets, at least the common datasets like people, people work on. so I guess that's, the two standards I would, I would impose. Yeah.

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: Do you think-- I have a question. Do you think like this is some like, Anton, if, if, if you have a good idea-

Zhuang Liu: Mm-hmm

Ravid Shwartz-Ziv: ... it should work on different domains, different datasets, different, uh, uh, places? Um, or like there are very good ideas that actually work on very specific, uh, scenarios.

So I do think both are valuable. I'm not, I'm not-- So that's a value of research, right? We, we-- You are given a... You are not required to be all successful at the, at the first step. Yeah. Though that would be good, but it's not a necessi-necessity. Yeah.

astra.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I think there are definitely very good ideas that work only in specific scenarios. I wouldn't say that every good idea has to work on vision and language and everything. Like, we just discussed, convolution has this locality, and that can be very useful for images. It doesn't have to be equally useful for every kind of data to be a good idea.

So I think it depends on what you're claiming, right? If you say you have a better general architecture, or a better replacement for some component that everybody uses, then I would want to see evidence in different settings. But if you're solving a particular problem, and the design makes sense for that problem, that's also very valuable.

The reason I like testing on multiple datasets is more to understand whether the improvement is reliable, whether we're learning something beyond the particular setting we tuned on. Those datasets could still be within the same domain. And, actually, understanding why something works in one setting but doesn't work in another can itself be very interesting. So, yeah, broad applicability is a nice property, but I wouldn't make that the definition of a good idea.

sol.text:
Yeah, I don’t think every good idea has to work everywhere. There can be very good ideas that address a very specific bottleneck—for example, long sequences, high-resolution images, or deployment on a particular type of hardware. And if the claim is scoped to that setting, that’s completely valid.

What bothers me more is when an idea is demonstrated in one narrow setting, but the conclusion is stated as if it is a general principle. If you claim a new fundamental architectural component is broadly better, then I would expect it to work across datasets, scales, and ideally different domains. If it only works in one regime, then we should try to understand what property of that regime makes it useful. That understanding can itself be a very valuable contribution.

So, yeah, I would say generality is not required for an idea to be good, but the evidence should match the scope of the claim. And usually, if you test on multiple settings, it also helps separate a real mechanism from something that happens to fit one particular training recipe or dataset. Yeah.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing broadly claimed principles across settings, but does not specifically require testing a domain-specific performance claim on multiple datasets within that scenario.

r003.rationale: It says that when an idea works only in one regime, researchers should understand what property of that regime makes it useful, providing the requested domain-specific explanation.

opus.text:
Yeah, that's, that's a good question. I think both exist, and, and I, I think the, the key is really about what claim you're making, right? So if, if someone says, "I have a domain-specific method, this is designed for, for medical imaging, or for, for protein structures," then, then of course they should just demonstrate it there, and that, that's completely, fine and, and honest. Like AlphaFold is, is extremely domain-specific, and, and it's one of the most impactful works, in, in deep learning, right? So I, I'm not saying everything has to be, universal. In fact a lot of, a lot of the most useful things are, are quite specific, like, tokenization tricks for language, or, or the, augmentation recipes in vision that don't, don't transfer at all to, to text.

What bothers me is when the claim is general, like, "this is a better way to parameterize a neural network," or, "this is a better normalization," or, "this is a better optimizer," and then it's only demonstrated on, on CIFAR, with one learning rate. Because the claim is, is about the fundamental mechanism, and then, the evidence is, is about one, one very narrow setting. And, my experience is that, most of those, don't survive. Like when, when you, when you move to another dataset or another scale, it, it just, goes away. So the, the level of generality of your evidence should, should match the level of generality of your claim. that's, that's kind of how I think about it.

And, and there's another thing I would add. I, I do think ideas that generalize across, across domains tend to be the ones that end up mattering more, in, in the long run, just because, they get adopted by more people and they compound with everything else. residual connections, attention, these, these are all, ideas that just work everywhere. but, but that's a statement about impact, not about, whether the work is good. Someone can do excellent work that, that only matters for, for one, one application. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. That’s a good question. I think it’s a bit of both.

If the idea is claiming to be a general thing — a better inductive bias, a better way to parameterize the network — then I do think it should tend to work on different domains, different datasets. That’s actually why residual connections and self-attention got adopted so widely, right? They just work in a lot of places. That’s also why I’m a fan of showing an idea on more than one dataset, not just the setting where you first saw the gain.

But I wouldn’t say every good idea has to work everywhere. There are definitely ideas that are very valuable in a specific scenario. ConvNets still excel when you’re in a vision-only setting, high resolution, local operations, easier to deploy. Transformers shine for unifying text and image, treating everything as tokens. Those are both good ideas, they just excel at different places.

So the key, for me, is matching the claim to the evidence. If you say this is a general architectural advantage, then yes, I want to see it in more than one domain. If it’s clearly scoped — this helps with this kind of data, this constraint, this task — that’s totally fine, and that can still be a very good idea. The problem is when something works in one specific setting, maybe even one hyperparameter recipe, and then gets written up as a general principle. That’s the confounding of architecture with recipe we were talking about.

Sometimes an idea starts specific and later transfers. Sometimes it doesn’t, and that also tells you something about the data and the inductive bias. So I wouldn’t require every idea to work on every dataset. I’d require the claim not to be more general than what you’ve actually shown. Yeah.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing general claims across multiple domains or datasets, but does not clearly require a scenario-specific performance claim to be tested on multiple datasets within that same scenario.

r003.rationale: The response discusses why ConvNets and Transformers excel in different settings, but does not state that domain-specific methods should be accompanied by an explanation of why they perform better in that domain.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I think it really depends on what the idea is claiming to be. 

If you are proposing what you claim is a fundamental principle or a core mechanism—like a new optimizer, a new normalization method, or a general alternative to residual connections or attention—then yes, I think it really should generalize across different datasets and different domains, like both vision and language. If a mechanism is truly fundamental to how neural networks learn, it shouldn't just be an artifact of one specific benchmark. If it only works on one benchmark or under very narrow conditions, it's very likely just overfitting to that specific setup or hyperparameter tuning.

On the other hand, I don't think every good idea has to be completely domain-agnostic. There are certainly very good ideas that rely on domain-specific inductive biases, and those are still extremely valuable. For instance, convolution incorporates locality and translation equivariance, which is naturally suited for images and 2D signals, even if it's not the best fit for language modeling. And those domain-specific designs can give you huge benefits in terms of efficiency, memory, and practical deployment for high-resolution vision tasks.

So I think both types of ideas are valid, but it's crucial to be honest and clear about the scope of the claim. If it's a domain-specific inductive bias, evaluate it thoroughly within that domain across multiple tasks; if it's claimed as a general architectural improvement, then it really needs to hold up across diverse domains.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says both general mechanisms and domain-specific inductive biases are valid and valuable ideas.

r002.rationale: It requires domain-specific ideas to be evaluated across multiple tasks within the domain, but does not clearly require testing across multiple datasets.

r003.rationale: It explains why a domain-specific method such as convolution performs well for vision: locality and translation equivariance suit images and 2D signals.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I, I think both can be true. I would say the, the very best ideas, the ones that really stand the test of time, they tend to be the ones that generalize, across domains, across scales, across modalities. Like, residual connections, self-attention, even normalization, these, these ideas just worked everywhere once they were proposed. Nobody expected transformers to, to take over vision when it first came out, right? So I think generality is kind of the, the ultimate evidence that an idea is, is real, that it's fundamental, and not just some artifact of, of a particular benchmark, or a particular hyperparameter setting. And, and this has a very practical side too, because if an idea only works on one small dataset, in, in one setting, it's very hard to distinguish whether it's a genuine improvement or just, you know, noise.

But, but on the other hand, I, I do think there are very good ideas that are specific to, to one domain. because the, the data in different domains have very different structures, right? Vision has, locality and, and translation invariance, language has this, sequential structure. So ideas that exploit these, these structures can be extremely useful in their own domain without, without transferring anywhere else. And, and I think that's fine, we shouldn't dismiss them just because they're not universal. I, I actually feel the community sometimes over-values universality, like everybody wants their idea to, to be the next transformer, to work everywhere. But that's, that's extremely rare, like once in five or ten years. Most progress is incremental and, and somewhat domain specific, and, and that is how the field actually moves forward.

So my, my rule of thumb is, you can claim different things, but the, the evidence should match the claim. If you claim it's a, a fundamental mechanism, then I want to see it on at least two very different settings, say vision and language. If you say it's a, a vision-specific improvement, then it's fine to just show it on vision, as long as, as you're honest about the scope. And, and the hard part is, verifying generality is expensive, which again comes back to, to the resource problem in academia we, we talked about. Actually this is something we thought about in our, in our own work on, on removing normalization, with, with dynamic tanh. One thing that really gave us confidence was that it worked across, across transformers, across vision models, across scales. That, that cross-domain validation is what convinced us it's, it's a real phenomenon rather than, than a trick. Yeah.

fable.text:
Yeah, that's a, that's a good question. I, I would say both, both exist. so, so if you look back at the ideas that really stayed with us, like residual connections, normalization, attention, Adam, these, these kind of things, they, they work everywhere, right? You put them in vision, you put them in language, you put them in speech, they, they just work. And I think that's, that's kind of the, the mark of a really fundamental idea. It, it doesn't care about the domain. It's addressing something about optimization or, or, how information flows through the network. So when I see an idea that works on ImageNet and also works on, on FineWeb, I, I tend to trust it much more.

but, but at the same time, I, I don't want to say every good idea has to be like that. there are ideas that are, are good precisely because they match the structure of the data. Like convolution is, is an example, right? It's, it's built for, images have this locality, translation, invariance, and, and it's, it's a very good idea for that. it, it doesn't really need to work on, on text to be, to be a good idea. Like, RoPE, position, positional encoding for, for language models, it's, it's specific to sequences. so I, I think there's, there's a difference between, domain-specific and, kind of, dataset-specific or, or setting-specific.

so what, what bothers me is, is not that the idea is, is specific to a domain. it's, it's when the idea is only, only working on one dataset with one set of hyperparameters at one scale. that, that's usually not a real effect. that, that's usually, the, the baseline was, was not tuned, or, or, there's something in the, in that particular dataset. So I, I guess my standard would be, if you claim the idea is general, then, then you need to show it on, on multiple domains. If, if you claim it's, it's for vision, or for, high resolution, or, for long context, then, then that's fine, but you should at least show it on multiple datasets within that domain, and, and at, at more than one scale. because the, the worst case is you, you find something that works at small scale, and then it, it just disappears when you scale up. we, we have seen a lot of this in, in the past, especially with, with architecture, papers. Yeah. So, so I don't require generality, but I, I require honesty about, about the scope. Yeah.

The response states that a claim of improved performance in a specific scenario should be tested on multiple datasets within that scenario.
The response states that a domain-specific method should be accompanied by an explanation of why it performs better in that domain.
